newsitem.title: USA: Globalization poses massive health threat - study.
newsitem.headline: Globalization poses massive health threat - study.

text.p: The surge in global trade and travel that is bringing people around the world closer together also is creating a huge health threat in the United States and other nations, a report issued on Saturday warned.

The biggest dangers come from the re-emergence of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis. The report, entitled "America's Vital Interest in Global Health," also cites problems caused by contaminated food and tainted consumer goods imported into the country.
And it mentions the threat of "germ warfare" as well as microbes resistant to antibiotics, such as Streptococcus, which causes pneumonia.
The report was issued by the Institute of Medicine, the medical arm of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences.
It calls for the creation of an early-warning system to detect newly emerging infectious diseases and other threats. Such a system also would organise international responses.

The Department of Health and Human Services would be the best agency to coordinate U.S. foreign assistance in the health field, according to the report. It charges that the U.S. government and businesses need to do to more to protect the American people as well as populations elsewhere.

"Because of our leadership in science and technology, the United States has a great deal to contribute to global health. And because of the increasing globalization of risks, it is in the United States' enlightened self interest to do so," said Barry Bloom, a professor at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York. He is co-chair of the Institute of Medicine's Board on International Health.
The value of international trade surged to $3.7 trillion in 1993 from $882.4 billion in 1975. Some two million peole cross an international border daily, according to the report.
More than 27 million Americans and Canadians travel to developing countries, and a growing number of visitors come to the United States. There were 115.5 million last year alone.

"Already, drug-resistant TB, which developed overseas, has become one of our major health problems in America. And this will occur with other diseases, one after the other, unless we act now," said Harvey Fineberg, Dean of the Harvard School of Public Health and also a Board co-chair.
The report lists a wide range of medical threats brought about by globalization:
-- The emergence of AIDS, which originated in Africa, as the No. 1 killer of young men aged 15-45 in the United States.
-- Cyclospora, a protozoan that came to New York and California from raspberries in Guatamala and sickened many people.

-- Aggressive and deadly new infections that jump from remote areas of the earth to modern cities. The Ebola virus recently was carried by a physician from Gabon to Johannesburg, South Africa, where it killed a nurse before doctors recognised it.
-- Travelers picking up age-old diseases such as malaria on trips overseas.
-- Mosquitoes capable of carrying dengue fever, viral encephalitis and yellow fever, which were introduced to the United States in 1985 through tires imported from Asia.
-- Pesticides banned in the United United but then found on imported food.
